data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided it is framed strictly as a methodological rule for selecting the most informative theory to subject to future falsification, rather than as a prediction of future success or an increase in probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that acting on corroboration requires an inductive assumption about the uniformity of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference leads to a pragmatic wager that implicitly assigns higher probability to the corroborated theory.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'methodological rule' and 'inductive inference' collapses when agents must act under uncertainty.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"This defense operates by distinguishing between 'corroboration' (a historical report of past performance) and 'verisimilitude' or 'probability' (claims about truth or future reliability). The mechanism relies on the asymmetry of risk: choosing a highly corroborated theory maximizes informational content and exposes the agent to the severest possible tests. If the theory fails, knowledge grows rapidly; if it survives, it remains the best available target for criticism. This avoids induction because the choice is not based on the expectation that the theory will continue to work, but on the logical necessity of testing the boldiest claims first.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
